text:
Video aged well(sort of). Their drivers increased performance 20+%(and 50% in some titles). I run an A770 16GB LE with my Gen9 I7 9700K@5GHz w/64GB XLR8 DDR4 - 3600(4x16GB dual channel), and M.2.
Even with the Z370 MSI(BIOS updated to latest in 2024) Gamer Pro is bottlenecking the card and M.2. Both are Gen4 and forced to Gen3. Indiana Jones The Great Circle is running incredibly on highest settings in 1080p. 1440p in low-mid settings. The 1080p maxed looks WAY better.
Yes, RT on just like the RTX 3060OC(8GB version was slightly slower than the A750 on Gen3). At least the ole' girl has Re-Bar, TPM 2.0, and Secureboot. Making this cobbled 2019-2022 parts custom never leaving me wanting for more. I only went from A750 to A770 for GDDR6 8 on A750 and 16 on A770 LE. And the 750 is Luna edition (white), and the 770 has RGB in the fan recesses and all around, plus top end. Looks 10x better in my system. My PC looks extremely high end, but is modest in specs.
Indiana Jones The Great Circle maxed on 1080p is 70-100fps. In 1440p low-mid is 55-70fps. 1080P looks gorgeous on my 165Hz Sansui Curved 1ms monitor. My buddy's 4K on the system in 1440p and 4K maxed was unplayable (8-25fps), but max setting in 1080p is barely lacking in quality. 4K gaming is just a way to see you more crap you don't need ..... IMO

text:
The fact that AMD cards spent so long in Driver hell, it's a great relief to see a simple DX9->DX12 translation layer being used for Intel's first gen. It's impossible to expect a first gen of GPUs to write 20+ years of graphics drivers all in one day, and this route is WAY better than glitchy native drivers. The fact that it's just a translation layer in the driver means the door is wide open for Intel to implement native DX9 support in their driver when Intel can dedicate the time for it.

Not even mentioning that Steam just pulled all support for CS:GO to run DX9! CS:GO 2 now runs DX11 and Vulkan.

text:
I did not pay a whole lot of attention to the FPS rates. But it seems to me to be a good thing to buy the 750. 

In "modern games" it performs at the level of a 3060. 

I put quotes around modern as my main game for instance is CIV6 which launched in 2016. It plays in DX11 or 12. So modern may be a bit of a stretch. I hate to look at the word recent too, as 2 years is a long time in computers. 8.5 years is forever.

Even bloons TD6 is a DX11 game. 

Resizeable bar. Also a little older than modern. I  feel comfortable calling it recent in computer history. A quick search shows the format was developed in 2008 but has been available in systems since 2020.

Why not buy it? 

If you still haven't completed (lol) CS:GO after nearly a decade. And you absolutely must have 400+ FPS. Then you need a more expensive card. 

I would look at some written reviews with more specs lists and such. Or hit one of the gaming framerate sites. And see how YOUR games perform and then pick up one of these if you need a new system or a video card now.

text:
Not quite the same as launching a product for Windows 12.

With Linux, you will eventually be able to upgrade to Linux 6 when your favourite distro comes around to it, and it isn't going to cost you a dime. But even without that, if you're a technically inclined user, you could just compile your own kernel and run Linux 6 yourself at any time.

Compiling your own kernel isn't for everyone for sure, but it's not actually that hard if you can follow a few instructions and have a little bit of technical experience with Linux.

Bleeding edge distros are already getting the new kernel soon anyway, while there are stable distros like Debian or Red Hat that takes their time, things can happen quite quickly in the other side of the Linux world.

See, I'm not sure the Linux support setup is actually a dealbreaker. Many Linux gamers (in the tiny market of Linux gamers that exist) already run on Arch, which will deliver 6.0 hot off the presses. Meanwhile, a lot of the issues around Arc are either mitigated or just a problem anyways. We don't have to worry about taking the hit on Intel's DX12 translation, because we do DX to Vulkan translation already anyways and take the hit for it on every vendor. But also, our old games use OpenGL, and the Iris OpenGL driver is in relatively good shape, or so I hear. 

So with everything looking the way it is, it's very possible that Arc is actually going to be a solid option for Linux gamers. Although I haven't checked Phoronix's analysis in detail yet.

Just saw the read more, it didn't show the first time I clicked. To be honest, it's not THEIR fault the cable melts (even though they could have some blame), the fault lies with the people who got the spec sheet and didn't even properly test it and made sure it didn't catch fire. Their cards are fine, the companies who made the cables didn't take the proper time and care to produce cables that can handle 600 watts constant for 10+-30+ hours. Yes, the pin size does lie with Nvidia, but the cable lies with the companies who made it. I didn't watch the Nvidia showcase thing cause I don't care for that, but I would assume that the card cools just fine and it's legit the cables that can't handle the absurd amount of wattage for 10+ hours. Melting is also the cable's fault for not being built good enough. Also, with the PSU, you cannot expect a PSU built from 10 years ago to support a current gen GPU. Eventually you need to upgrade things, and having that upgrade ensures that everything will be compatible. Hell, I wouldn't want a PSU from 10 years ago running in my system I have right now. That'd be asking for trouble. The size of the card also cannot be controlled as if you want more of something, you need to get bigger to accommodate it. Like literally any black hole, they become more destructive/stronger the bigger they are. Yes, Nvidia could find ways to reduce the size and stuff, but it's going to take time and we will eventually end up back at square one. GPUs are not going to stop getting bigger and bigger, they may reset in size eventually, but they will always continue to become bigger when we pack more stuff into them, even after Nvidia has found a way to reduce the size of the GPU.

text:
When one of my main games went from DX9 to DX11 basically nothing happened. It didn't look any better, it didn't perform any better. The only difference was that it now required a DX11 capable card. In fact, a year later they managed to destroy performance on quad cores with an update. Yes, a game that transitioned to DX11 in 2019.
It will take years of preperation in advance before you can throw out the old stuff. If the new hardware performs worse than the old one, but offers the ability to run ahead 2-3 years later, why buy it.
And that is basically what happened here. They took away with hardware support for older APIs, which in turn caused the card to perform badly in those older APIs. And since the games I play are basically exclusively DX8, DX9 or DX11, Arc for me is dead on release and not worth the money. If further down the line I play more DX12 games for which my current card isn'T fast enough, i might consider getting one of the Intel cards. But at this point in time it would be wasted.

Okay, no. The competition argument has not, and will not, ever hold up.

Here's the thing, if you accept inferior products for the sake of competition, then you're still behaving like you're in a monopoly. Monopolies are not bad per se and people need to understand that. There's nothing morally wrong with them. The reason monopolies are problematic is that the free market can only operate effectively if companies are forced to compete with one another. Market forces operate by consumers choosing the options that most suits them. The problem with not going for the best option is that in such a situation, there still is no competition, because the losers can just rely on the monopoly argument instead of actually competing, and the winners still have their market share for being better by default, cause the losers aren't improving. You've still got a stagnating market, just now with a Monopoly Under The Monopoly.

text: The thing is, it need to translate the old code to the new one while running. But you have to limit the amount of translations so that it will give you reasonable performance while the game itself runs right behind it. So when a big scene appear and needed to be load constantly, your CPU has to load both of the heavy load at the same time, plus Windows and the balancer to make sure the game at least won’t crash. So basically, it will eat an overhead of twice or more the processing power and space to process both the present and the future codes at once. You can’t delegate much of this onto other places as it will exponentially increase the complexity demanded in the translator and balancer.

text:
Yes it will, but by that time the Used Market will be flooded while the New Cards will be getting discounts. And the next-gen cards after would be getting ready for release.

The point is always be careful about "future-proofing" your system. Sure there's certain things you should do, but the gist is paying more today for a promise tomorrow rarely works out.

With all that said, Intel stuffed up their opportunity. They needed to release this in 2019 and made on their own favs. That way it would have been competitive performance wise against the RDNA-1 and RTX-20 cards. Then it would've been competitive during the 2020-2022 run. Intel lost the chance to make alot of money. And in 2023 they could've been competitive value-wise.

The other big point, is that they could have shifted Intel-Foundry to focus primarily on GPU, SSD, RAM, Motherboard manufacturing and also external chip orders. While their more crucial products could have been outsourced to the technically superior TSMC-Node to stay competitive. Imagine their Core-i7 and Core-i9 chips easily surpassing Ryzen 7 and Ryzen 9 processors. While their Core-i3 and Core-i5 could still be built inhouse and offer strong value-for-money. Big wasted opportunity there.

text:
Been running Linux kernel 6.0 since  rc3, so I'm not worried about that. The Linux kernel 6.0 being compared to Windows 12 is disingenuous, though, because the Linux kernel's release cadence is far higher (when Windows 10 was released, the kernel was on version 4.2. When Win 11 released, the kernel was on version 5.14, with 5.15 in final release candidates). Ubuntu and the like typically stick with the LTS kernel, which is closer to Windows' biannual major upgrades. The most recent LTS is 5.15, released in October 2021. In all likelihood, either 6.0 or 6.1 will be christened as the newest LTS after a few minor versions, and I would therefore expect Ubuntu 23.04 and similar to ship with it. And realistically, anyone who is looking to pick up an Intel card and running Linux is technical enough to at least track down a guide for how to upgrade the kernel on their distro of choice.

For myself, I'm seriously considering it. Phoronix's testing shows the A770 falling between the 6600XT at the high end and the RTX 3060 at the low end (with some tests even challenging the 6700XT and the 3070), and I badly want to ditch Nvidia for my primary GPU. Luckily, my mobo supports ReBar with my 1600X.

text:
Yeah, when Intel stars adding a more diverse cooler, backplate, and colors, then I might buy them.
Yes, none of those are legitimate reasons to pick out a card, but when you have a theme, or God forbid, you decide to build an all white PC, these things matter.
Got a black case with a tinted side panel window and all red case fans and red LED strips? You're probably going to go the extra mile and buy an MSI GPU that has the iconic black are red cooler on it along with a black or black and red motherboard with a few white accent pieces here and there. Possibly even going for RGB ram sticks and cable extensions most likely from either cable mod or asia horse.
For the, realistically, average buyer, they aren't going to know what they are getting and shill out what little money they have for a prebuilt with 3 RGB fans, a glass front panel so they can see them, and an old CPU paired with a 1650 all because it said i7 and it said it has a graphics card + the pretty lights.
With Intel being the newcomer, they are not only tied to their primary product line (CPU production), but their reputation is also on the line as well. This being a direct problem for them because they need to look professional and seeing that most prebuilds do not have an Intel GPU in them, PC enthusiasts and custom PC builders will be the majority of their audience. While they may be the target audience, their brand is still more of a XEON style while the target audience is full send FPS. What I'm trying to say is that they need to look professional while their audience is most likely looking at other AIBs like EVGA, Zotac, Asus, MSI, etc because the coolers have all these random unnecessary things tacked on that their audiences are specifically looking for.
Now Intel's line up has become significantly slimmer in terms of buyers because in order to move product, they need to produce a card that is cheap enough, yet good enough to compete with NVIDIA and AMD. Who is their new target audience? Newcomers in the PC building scene who grew up with intel computers both at school and at home. "If it was good everywhere else in life, why not in my new PC? And they make graphics cards now! They're cheap enough to play the small library of games that I have and I can't afford a monitor that can output 100+ frames per second anyway."
Seriously, if they want to make a splash, they'll need to make an edgier cooler design to appeal to the larger audience.

To anyone wondering why I said, "God forbid, an all white PC", it's because white parts are especially niche and expensive because the audience looking to buy those parts is much smaller and thus low demand means increased prices. If most motherboards are black now, white ram sticks will stand out and clash with the rest of the build. Thus further decreasing the draw to white parts. What about cleaning? Black will look cleaner longer because you won't see the dust building up nearly as quickly as white will.
And yes, I do know this from experience. My current system is running all white parts. I tried really hard to avoid it and go full send on performance only, but I wanted all white bad enough that I spent the extra time and money saving to get all white components.

To anyone looking to build a PC, it's extremely easy to waist money and unnecessary things in a computer. You can save loads of money by getting the cheapest version of whatever GPU you're trying to get. Instead of getting RGB fans, controllers, RGB RAM, colored cable extensions, an ATX motherboard, and a 3 fan GPU littered with RGB (let's say a 3060), you could instead get an mATX motherboard with built in WIFI and Bluetooth, a 3070, a smaller case to take up less space, larger capacity RAM (preferably a matching kit of 2 or 4) and a higher tier CPU.
I spent about 2k on my PC to get 32gbs of ram, a i5-12600k, and a RTX 3060. I could have easily done so much better had I gone with none white parts, non RGB everything, 2x16gb stick of ram instead of the 4x8 I went with, and so much more. But, more expensive parts do have their own perks to them too. I have all my dim slots populated with RGB ram, nearly every single fan I have is controlled by the AIO and fan hub that came with my Corsair AIO so I didn't have to worry about having enough fan headers on my motherboard, and I have the best looking PC out of all my friends. Does that last part help my get better in games? No. But now I can watch myself loose in 100+ fps with rainbows all over the place or blinding white light in my eyes.

text:
11:10 You can't compare Linux 6 to Windows 12, that's not how it works. The issue is that you can't add new in-tree drivers to already released kernels in a patch release, the drivers have to be added in a new kernel release, and Linux 6 is pretty much the next kernel release. So Intel simply can't add drivers to already released kernels (unless they are out-of-tree drivers, but that's another can of worms), unlike in your Windows comparison and given how drivers are handled on Windows.
Also, the Linux kernel number changing from 5 to 6 has no significance, it was arbitrary decided, it might as well have been called 5.20, i.e. there are no grand changes in there that really necessitate a number change but devs just felt like they have been using number 5 for too long now.

That doesn't prevent them from making drivers. Drivers can be done as modules which are loaded dynamically, they don't have to be part of the kernel. They can have drivers in the kernel since version 6 but they can have drivers as modules for whatever version in the past.

text:
After 40+ years of computers, these days I don't sign up to be a beta-tester, or effectively one. In fact, I would pay hundreds of dollars for stability and reliability then have to depend on ANY company's tech support which is always a dice-roll in terms of responsiveness, expertise and attitude. It used to be that at least some of the tech support personnel were genuine geeks who would work with me to help diagnose and fix a problem (going the extra mile if necessary). However, these days the rule is non-techies using trouble-shooting flow charts. And I don't mind "English as a 2nd Language," but this can turn into a nightmare if the phone connection quality sucks. 

Finally, with a lot of tech support moved to India or similar parts of the world, half the time there exists a palpable lack of respect, if not distain, because I'm a woman and therefore obviously an idiot. In fact, it can get ugly with them abandoning helping me with my tech problem for the clearly more important task of "reminding me of my place." I started to experience the above situation some 10-20 years ago and it has only gotten more frequent with time. To be clear, I have had delightful exceptions (respect, expertise, good phone connection quality, a "can-do" attitude, etc.), but again, I'm entirely at their mercy and the exceptions are becoming more rare by the year  :-(

I do like that there is now 3-way competition for graphics cards and once Intel gets its driver situation sorted, I would consider their products (especially in light of Nvidia's horrid treatment of its partners, venders, employees, etc.). 

That said, I believe that we must also consider that it is not uncommon for companies to dip a toe into the water, not see an avalanche of profits, and then kill that part of their business. Thus, there is always the risk of being an early adopter and then get stuck with a suddenly unsupported piece of hardware (and few companies in this situation behave like EVGA and offer refunds to people that purchased extra warrantees, hold back cards for warranty replacements, and otherwise act in an ethical manner, putting their customers first.)

text:
"I think the main issue with Intel's design is that they really built everything around new systems and technologies.": Except, they didnt build it "around" it at all.

Firstly, Keep in mind, Re'Bar is a hardware level /flag/ (enables memory mapping), In theory you could enable it on even older GPU's if the hardware was capable of mapping more then 256mb chunks. | The only reason why this wasnt done before, is that the GPU hardware engineers have been dragging their knuckles since 2011... With Gimmicks taking place sensible improvements to a standard from 2003...
Secondly, Intel /needs/ Re'Bar as its drivers are so poor, it lacks a appropriate pixel pipeline to access data fast enough without it. This is where we get into root of all issues.

Intel's didnt come with DX12, or the Next Mainline Linux Kernel in mind. Its a result of them dumping 15 years of driver development from earlier products. right in the rubbish bin.
DX12(and vulkan, that its a clone of) is by far the /simplest/ implementation for a graphics pipeline. Why? Nearly all calls are /hardware/ calls. Unlike previous generations (DX5-11), Where all calls were first processed by the CPU and used the driver to translate the calls to work the hardware could do. DX12/Vulkan sheds all of this, and does it in a un-intuitive way.

In the old days, there was a severe lack of standardization. Game developers were always trying to find new ways to get around hardware limitations to perform complex drawing and mapping, that we take for granted today. Until as early as DX9, nearly all calls were hardware/vendor specific for DX. Meaning while a driver could emulate functions, you would often get different result between different vendors. 
By DX10/11, the hardware and game engine routines were all pretty much a set standard that implement across every brand pretty evenly...

Moving back to the topic, because this new driver doesnt build on a existing, Implementing DX5-11 would be a lengthy and incredibly ardious job. While you could (relatively) easily remap the older drivers functional calls into a psuedo-interface for the DX12 renderer pipeline. Intel thought "Microsoft and Mesa already did this, there is no point in doing it twice!", and it typical INTEL fashion, yeeted 15 years of both in-house and community work out the window.

Now we get to the real issue. Intels DX12 driver, is /basic/. While it does most of the main calls necessary for expected base functionality. It ignores any calls that it doesnt have added yet or the hardware lacks firmware instructions to draw... This is why when we get the live-stream, closer eyed viewers are going to notice something unexpected. The cards dont render the same. Intel is getting better framerates by dropping "Unnecessary" calls, to overcome poorly made drivers...

---

Then we finally get to the Linux topic. | Linux is not like windows. Versioning is done in steps, and new features/drivers are not usually "Backported" to older kernel versions. This ensures that stability and performance expectations can remain and provides a easy way to review for regressions (Something microsoft has always failed on horribly).

As a result, Intel is not "updating" their previous generation of drivers, or just sliding in new device support to a list. Its a entirely /new/ driver.

As such, Torvalds only lets new features and drivers get added to upcoming releases for review before being finalized. Its not unusual for newly added features and drivers to sit a year or more until it reaches a release candidate. | Sometimes drivers are backported in, but only under some extreme pressure.

That said, Kernel version 6.x is already deployed in many rolling-release distributions. What linus was talking about more applies to /staged release distributions/ like Debian and Ubuntu where software updates take upwards of 3 years to trickle into their releases. As their goal is completely stable releases, at the cost of functionality and performance. Even incompatibility on newer hardware.

Fedora would be next in line, but due to scheduling, it won't arrive until Fedora 38, and Fedora 37 isn't even out of beta yet, which means a half-year wait. It's even worse for Ubuntu users, who have to deal with both a similar scheduling issue as Fedora on top of already tending to use older kernels than other distros, which will affect other ubuntu-based distros like Mint, Zorin, and Pop OS.

Just for the record, when ignoring Steam OS (since practically noone's gonna run that on an Arc GPU anyway), Linux gamers are going to be using primarily Ubuntu kernels, followed by Arch kernels, and apart from maybe Gentoo users, most of them are going to stick to the stable branch. This means at best, they're already gonna have to wait an entire month to use an Arc GPU, but most of everyone else will be waiting a bit over 6 months to use an Arc GPU.

Especially given Linux's popularity with people that do AI work, and Intel is trying to market this card towards these people in particular... not the best move.


All of that aside, the lowest end model really does seem like a super compelling option as an encoding GPU for streamers. I'm interested in what the results will be in that video.

text:
As somebody who bought AMD for years, mainly just to see shader crashes... I'm really looking forward to the second generation of these cards; if Intel pursues software stability and general bug-fixing like it does for its CPUs and motherboards, ARC may very well mean that there's an exciting option coming, and I strongly suspect that the cards aren't entirely slower due to silicon; they're simply seeing the huge learning-cliff between them and their rivals, in terms of drivers and integration w/ Windows. 

I'm not buying the first generation, though; when GPU prices became less ridiculous, we bought all the rendering horsepower we'll need for another year or two, and all of it was nVidia this round, because AMD's offerings were so... meh, in terms of performance per dollar. ARC's prices make a lot more sense.

I just hope Gelsinger realizes that GPUs aren't something that Intel can get right immediately and looks at this as a 10-year project, rather than presuming that if the numbers suck in a couple of quarters that ARC's just doomed as a concept; AMD really does appear to be (finally) getting their software working decently and catching up to nVidia on speed, so this may become a very exciting time for consumers.

text:
​ @animejanai4657  This is the most cherrypicked AMD fanboyism I have ever seen. Babteltechreview did some real benchmarks. And they came to this conclusion:

"The performance of the latest AMD Software Adrenalin 22.7.1 driver was like a roller coaster. Based on our previous results and findings, although we saw some significant and notable performance gains using the latest 22.7.1 driver compared to 22.6.1 drivers, we still see significant performance inconsistencies and notable performance regressions that prevent us from recommending 22.7.1 for general or global use for Radeon users. Therefore, our current recommended driver for RDNA 2.0 gamers is still the Adrenalin 22.6.1 Optional driver or WHQL AMD’s Recommended 22.5.1 drivers for the best functional stability."

For everyone who wonders which game it was that AMD claimed the increase? It was Minecraft in 4k.

Overall the performance increases in paper but there are also a lot of losses. Days Gone even loses 31% P.01 FPS. Doom Eternal on the other hand got P.02 61% increase. But most changes are between 5% loss and 10% gain. Biggest problem I see is the distribution. In most cases only the average FPS goes up and in turn min FPS goes down. Which is really bad.

And no I don't count increases in GravityMark. Nobody plays GravityMark. People play games.

So. If you play Cyberpunk 2077, Doom Eternal or Minecraft in 4k the 22.7.1 is for you. In any other game tested the performance got worse.

People really need to stop with this blind and irrational fanboyism. Keep it real. AMD isn't on your side. They only try to take the moral highground is because they are the underdogs right now. The second AMD reaches 60% market shares they will be a moralless shithole as any other company out there. Stop being emotionally attached to ANY company. They only care for money. Everything else is just business strategy. And you have proven to fall for that.

text:
When it comes to Linux support: sadly that is to be expected. Every new kernel version has feature freeze weeks before its release, which means no new hardware enablements unless it's done early. Intel was posting their patches for months now, but the more-or-less complete support was only ready for the 6.0 feature window.

The comparison to "drivers only for Windows 12" is simply incorrect. Linux 6.0 was released last Sunday (02.09.2022) and it's 'mainline' version - which means it's not testing version or release candidate, but stable version. Also Linux being the only one component of the GNU/Linux system makes it possible to use the new kernel with ANY Linux distro, even not the freshest one (although it might require compiling it). Moreover, rolling release (like Arch or OpenSuse Tumbleweed) will have it their stable channels in matter of days. Wanna use something more conservative for the sake of robustness? Sorry, that's how things look on that front. You simply don't put the Debian Stable on a bleeding edge hardware expecting it to work correctly out-of-the-box, that's how it always worked. If you use something like that, go compile newest kernel and Mesa.

author: @MistyKathrine

text:
@MistyKathrine  Long story short, because of the way the shaders have to compile, you can occasionally see through solid objects until they load in.

Also, it's technically a .dll hook, which some cheat protection engines just red flag immediately. (I think Punkbuster used to pass out kicks/bans for using Rivatuner on-screen display, for example.)
author: @Hyatice

text: @Hyatice  Odd.  If it becomes a thing that's needed for intel GPUs, there would probably be pressure from intel to not ban people for it.
author: @MistyKathrine

text:
​ @MistyKathrine  It is odd, but at the end of the day if DXVK (an open-source project largely manned by a single individual, which has to translate DX commands to Vulkan) can do a better job than Intel's DX to DX translation layer, something is up..

The running theory as to why DXVK can get better performance on the low-end (iGPU) hardware is that Vulkan has significantly lower CPU requirements. If a game is GPU bound, you're likely to see a performance decrease or stay the same. If a game is CPU bound (or if you're using a low total power limit - in the case of handhelds or possibly some thermal throttled gaming laptops, for example), you'll likely see a significant performance uplift.

If the DXVK translation layer can reduce CPU load but the DX9/10/11 > DX12 translation layer that Intel is using increases CPU load, it seems entirely possible that DXVK would be useful here.

Source: Just tinkering as a handheld PC enthusiast. Up til the 6800U, there hasn't really been a compelling reason to use AMD in the handheld space as Xe was surprisingly out-competing Vega in everything except broad compatibility.. And DXVK was one of the tools in the toolkit for stuff that Xe didn't like.

Only supporting Linux 6.0+ isn't thaaat big of a deal. It's mostly akin to releasing drivers late.

text: ​ @Dwayneff  That's actually my current card and i have 0 complaints about it. Ok maybe one that it was defaulted on performance mode and i want my games to look as good as possible but you can change absolutely everything in settings and for each game separately! Im not a ridiculously huge frames per second guy im more of a lowest possible latency with the best looks at stable 60 fps kinda guy. If you aim for that go to nvidia control panel lock your frames at 60 and set your vsync on fast mode. This way your gpu remains cold and silent when doing trivial stuff and gets the job done in graphically advanced games! I even play some games at 2560x1600 or some old games at 2880x1800 it is far more superior than any antialiasing mode at my native resolution (1920x1200) I still use AA on these big ass resolutions haha. text:
Comparing the Linux situation to Windows 12 is a bit extreme. Intel & AMD put their drivers directly in the kernel itself, so it is tied to the kernel version. Stable release linux distros have an option to switch to "rolling" kernel updates, or may just roll kernel updates anyways. It may be a month or 2, but it will be available soon. And if you are on Arch, you could temporarily switch to the linux-mainline kernel in the AUR, but problems may occur.

I will also note that it is important to include the .0 in 6.0, as the only significance in bumping the major version is that the number after the dot looks "too big".

This was why, even though the VIC-20 had 5 Kilobytes of RAM, we could use only 3,583 of those 5K of RAM. The Video Interface Chip (VIC) reserved 1,417 of those 5,000 bytes of RAM.

text: To raise the understanding (and tolerance) there is a dark art to high performance device drivers and especially so in gaming graphics. The interface between the "app" (game) and the bits between it and the hardware must be very highly tuned.  A lot of non-GPU device drivers are "whatever they are" as no one is looking under the hood or pushing the efficiency. In fact efficiency is the challenge here. Low Level programmers (a specific skill set that is not common at all) have to use "performance analyzers" to identify where the code is spending  too much time. They then look at the modules and figure out how to squeeze every instruction and delay out of it. Most of the time this turns into assembly language programming for ideal optimization. That's level's below a high level language. In fact most programmers never know what CPU instructions actually run and some high level languages have popular constructs that are not efficient at all.  They will test the defined module's edges and what goes on inside is a "black box".  For GPU drivers, since the GPU hardware is an autonomous compute entity - they have to double down on this optimization. They must optimize on the CPU side and again on the GPU side and make them sing together. No trivial challenge. AND of course every game developer is also looking for hooks that are faster and may be up to their own optimizations.  We all saw how bad AMD drivers were for a while there and every new architecture has its early adopter pains and of course legacy to support. Its a real challenge even if you have a "10X" low level programmer who can jump between the unique worlds / stacks.  It SEEMS that Intel's hardware, although late and dated (originally targeting the RTX2000 series) and thus already a gen behind, is solid, scalable and very conservative. The challenge will be getting over this learning curve and  laying a solid foundation for future enhancement.  They of course also may have to embrace the work going on in the foundries team at some point which in itself could glitch them further.

text:
This is excellent to finally see the Arc A7 coming through and broadly living up to expectations. With driver updates it should hopefully become better.

I'm not in the market for one (have 3060ti) and enthusiasts and competitive gamers would straight up laugh at it, however this is the most important GPU launch for decades. Nvidia and AMD have absolutely screwed the budget/mainstream end of the market for too long, pricing the lower end of the market way too high and giving lacklustre upgrades. For example I had a regular 1660 and the regular 3060 is barely 30% more powerful. The 1660 cost me £200 and the 3060 is a minimum of £320. That's why for the first time, I had to go higher than a regular 60 series card and go for the 3060ti. The 3050 is just an insult.

If things carry on as they are, too many gamers will be priced out of worthwhile upgrades like they have been this generation. Eventually the bottom will just fall out of the market and PC gaming will become a pastime afforded only by the rich whilst the poors have to make do with consoles. PC gaming is in a great place right now with an unprecedented amount of ports from console, Japanese games and indies, growing to this stage thanks to a previously decent price/performance ratio of PC builds and GPUs compared to what consoles were offering. We need this growth to continue and Arc is hopefully the answer, to at least put pressure on Nvidia/AMD to improve their lower end cards dramatically.

With Intel's aggressive presence in the OEM market for CPUs, they should be able to leverage this for Arc too.

text:
Some clarification on the linux support, this is NOT a fault on intel.
It is simply how stable linux distributions work. They do not get feature updates, especially for things like the kernel.
Whenever these distributions get a new release they will ship a kernel that is up-to-date for that time.
For ubuntu this will be somewhere this fall.
If you want an arc card before that on linux try something like arch and derivates( >> garuda, manjaro), opensuse-tumbleweed or any other rolling release.
(This is also the main reason why some people like rolling releases)
Alternatively you can also install a newer kernel manually on any distribution.

text:
Just like everyone else seems to be doing, I have a few issues regarding parts of this video.

My main one is the blender results.
Blender isn't like a video game, you cannot just do one set of settings for all GPU's.
Different GPU manufacturers have settings specific to their device.

Its like if a game had an amd settings, and nvidia setting, and an intel setting, BUT you tested all three GPU's in Nvidias mode and concluded nvidia wins. Its not saying anything about the actual performance of the hardware.
Heck, different architectures from a single manufacturer or even the same architecture but different GPU can be optimized while getting the same exact render in the end.

By not telling us what settings you use, or the blender version(huge strides are being made for optimizing for amd over the past year or two) the test is useless for people trying to evaluate the performance of the GPU for blender and non blender users. And by not optimizing for each gpu the test is even more useless.

Nvidia absolutely wins vs AMD on the newest version of blender from what little information I can find on the subject but 0 people with intel GPU's in hand have done proper blender tests.

text:
The Linux 6.0 to Windows 12 comparison is not really valid.. It may seem like Linux 6.0 is a major new version compared to 5.19, but it's just another minor revision. After 20 minor versions, the "major" version number is incremented but it's not a special release. So we had 3.0-3.19, then 4.0-4.19, then 5.0-5.19, and now 6.0.

Patch updates to an existing kernel release (e.g. 5.19.12 to 5.19.13) are only made for bug fixes. It's not like Intel could backport the driver to earlier Linux versions but didn't want to. They can only add it to the next minor version, which at this time happens to be 6.0.

It will of course take time for releases of stable distributions that start out with a 6.0 kernel to be the norm. Updating the kernel to 6.0 in these distributions may have its pitfalls. author: @peshozmiata

text:
@DrakyHRT  I wouldn't be so quick to dismiss OpenGL.  A big part of the issue is OpenGL implementations on Windows tend to be pretty subpar.  AMD's OpenGL implementation is terrible on Windows.  NVIDIA's is pretty solid on both platforms.  Mesa's OpenGL implementation for AMD on Linux is much better than the official Windows implementation.  Intel's OpenGL on Linux is also Mesa and there are a lot of shared optimizations among Mesa/Gallium3D drivers, plus Mesa also has Zink (OpenGL-on-Vulkan) which has been making pretty good strides in performance too.

Even on Windows, I have no doubt that a D3D9 to DX12 wrapper could work well, it's just a matter of implementation.  DXVK and VKD3D have been doing the 3D API wrapper thing pretty well for a while now.

I think as a tech enthusiast, what use case people don't realize Arc could be REALLY GOOD for is troubleshooting in general.

Many people don't have access to having a "spare GPU" lying around for testing graphics issues, and don't want to default to using iGPUs for testing (since raytracing is not possible there).

Intel makes a strong case selling the Arc series for ~$300 because it's a lot easier to justify spending that on a backup for troubleshooting than it is to shell out double, or even triple, for feature parity purposes.

I might pick one up for that reason. I may not use it much, but when I need to test an issue, you better believe that it will come in handy

text: The Linux 6–Windows 12 comparison is complete, 100% BS. First: Linux is gratis, so you don't have to pay for the newest release. Second: On Linux you get frequent updates to the kernel — even between major releases, so you will have it soon, and you will not have to reinstall your computer. Third: The desktop and the kernel are not bundled on Linux, so an upgrade to the Linux 6 doesn't affect your desktop experience. Fourth: Windows 12 has not been announced whereas Linux 6.0 has already been released and you can install it on whichever distribution you want (on this point a comparison to Windows 11 would be more accurate).

text:
12:30 Criticizing a company for raising prices during periods of absurdly high demand and short supply is an odd and a bit naive critique to make. Virtually every business does this, and for good reason.

Raising prices weeds out the consumers who really don't want or need the product bad enough, and helps fund production to meet demand. Where under normal conditions, some sources of material or manufacturing may not be viable for the cost, it now is when consumers are willing to pay more. They can then take advantage of these usually cost-prohibitive sources to pump out more products.

The alternative to not raising prices means stock is even more sparse as less is being produced and it is all immediately bought up, and then just gets jacked up in price by scalpers on the second hand market anyhow.

It's much better off for the companies actually developing these products to be the beneficiaries of higher prices than it is for the jackoffs who are just capitalizing off a shortage and not actually producing anything.

A good example of a company that refuses to increase their prices is Vivo barefoot, a shoe company. I've wanted some for quite some time. So have many other people. Yet they're literally never in stock, so it's impossible for me to get the pair I want, even if I am willing to pay double the price.

text:
You know what I was REALLY hoping for in ARC, considering they did GVT-g before, and Intel would've had no competition in the space if they had went for it on their most recent tech? vGPU. They would've caught NVIDIA and AMD both out of left field, and they had nothing to lose, because they don't have any overpriced professional-tiered cards to sell.

Especially since Arc's about the best VRAM-per-buck ratio card you can get right now. It'd be the professional GPU to get, if the drivers got up to snuff.

They have to enable SR-IOV in a driver update. I would not hesitate to buy an Arc GPU if that happened. An important chunk of the Linux community is wishing for this.

Also, I'm betting Intel is relying on the community to do the driver backporting for them. Linux 6.0 is not a major update, and the drivers are open source.

Edit: SR-IOV upstream task is on-going according to Kris Pan @ Intel. ETA Q4'23. They have a Windows VM they're testing with, and it's working well.
Source: linux-intel-lts issue 33 on GitHub.
However, they're likely working on the integrated Xe GPUs and not ARC. Hopefully the architecture isn't different enough and the same SR-IOV driver works for both.

text:
I'll put on my shill hat for a moment too, so take this with a grain of salt.

These arc GPU chips are actually massive, with a much better node than what Intel uses to produce CPUs. There's a lot of silicon there. If the results are lackluster, then chances are it is mostly because of drivers.
If intel keeps this product around for years, chances are we are going to see massive gains for the performance of these cards as drivers and the software matures. When Linus says that the cards are a gamble - he's right. They are a gamble, and perhaps for the average gamer the upside isn't all that big. For anyone who does any kind of AI work, the upside is potentially absolutely massive.

If electricity prices keep going up, maybe I'll look at what's the most energy efficient solution, but for now I can't justify purchasing this intel GPU no matter how much I want to.

If your intention is to only play newer dx12 games and some other esports titles then i think ARC would be an okay buy.
It certainly is difficult recommending it over the RX6600, but I can see ARC being sold and not just collect dust on shelves.

Personally, as someone who recommends PC Hardware to their friends, I am in a difficult situation. I want people to get the best bang for their buck and face the least issues possible, but I also want the ARC stuff to be sold.

It ultimately comes down to people who are savvy and don't mind little bits of hiccups so that they can support good competition in the market.

ARC sure is a confusing proposition, but it is very important that intel doesn't leave this market and delivers more competitive products in the future.

text: I think a large portion of the reason why Intel Optane died off was related to how few PCIe lanes Intel themselves were willing or able to cram into their consumer processors, particularly for mobile chips. Had they doubled up the number of lanes for storage devices in the 8th-10th gen so every laptop could be made with two direct-attached NVMe storage devices then it probably would have worked out differently. But when you're forced to choose between a 128GB optane stick and a 1TB NVMe SSD, well, the choice becomes obvious. Hopefully they'll end up selling their portion off to Micron so the tech can see another generation.

text: The Linux support discussion is really poor here. Linux 6.0 is not like windows 12 at all. Linux 6.0 is just the next version from 5.19, Linus just changes the major number once in a while. Linux distributions also pick up the new kernel versions very quickly and the kernel is always backwards compatible. So if you need Linux 6.0 today you can just install a newer kernel. For most users the next version of their favorite distribution will just have this included and for something like Ubuntu even the Long Term Support version will get this backported. So to use the Windows analogy it's like having to wait for the next release of Windows 10.

author: @guyguy463

text: @ykai89  You say that, but the entire fricking open-source Python, Julia, R, etc. ecosystems are basically driven by academia. A lot of academics may not mind using proprietary software when they can afford it and it gets the job done, but clearly the stereotype for academia is still to struggle financially and a lot of times having an open system is part of getting the job done.
author: @neolexiousneolexian6079

text: @ykai89  often times, academics write their own software to avoid crazy expensive licenses and slow software. For my research, no other CFD software could do the job in time. Even Ansys, which is $120k/license, is about a factor 200 slower than my own software on the same hardware. We researchers don't have an infinite money supply for overpriced software and Quadro/Tesla GPUs, and even more we don't have infinite time to wait for painfully slow software like MATLAB. Competitively priced gaming GPUs benefit us too.
author: @ProjectPhysX

text:
​ @neolexiousneolexian6079  I do recognise those project and the excellent work done with and by them. Just sharing what I'm seeing anectodally. And I think it's not just me given how dominant CUDA is. There are a lot of academics who care about open-source but there are also a lot who just want something that allows them to meet their publication KPIs. It'd be great if OpenCL vs CUDA can end like how Freesync did with Gsync, but I'm not sure if that'll be anytime soon. 

Having more open systems for research and laboratory testing is definitely a good thing. There is also a similar issue in medical devices. Vendors are locking off their products and making massive margins because most of the users in these spaces are funded by governments and multinationals.

text: @ProjectPhysX  That sounds great! I'll say the ones I observe aren't exactly academics who are doing bleeding edge ML or computation/simulation research. 1) buy an intel/amd gpu to "encourage" competition

2) buy the best brand new gpu for $300

3) buy the best gpu for $300, PERIOD (used included).


Imo.. the best choice is #3, the second best is #2. The worst option is to buy a gpu based on which company you like, or to "encourage" competition.  The term "best" here is subjective. IMO best the the total user experience. So HYPOTHETICALLY, if AMD offered better rasterized performance in all the games you play, but the drivers were unstable.. and Nvidia offered 10% worse raterized performance, but with stable hassle free drivers.. imo Nvidia would be the way to go. That's more likely than 3 companies surviving in the GPU market where all the wealthy kids get Nvidia GPUs.

The 2nd best selling GPU on Amazon when I checked was an AIB 3090 Ti.

You can see from that how people view AMD and how they view Nvidia.  The best selling AMD GPU is a 6600, and the 2nd best selling Nvidia GPU is a 3090 Ti.

So no, you'll probably still have a duopoly, and it will be much worse.

text: Duopolies are what market forces almost always end up creating. When products competing for the same market are offered in every region, there will almost always be two major players. When there are three (or more) competitors, one will slip into (or beyond) a distant 3rd and become almost irrelevant. In CPUs we used to have Intel AMD and Cyrix, now it's just Intel and AMD. In consoles there are many examples such as the Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis trading blows while everyone else that generation remained irrelevant. Or how the N64 and Playstation duked it out while Sega's offering languished a distant 3rd. There are many others like that.
